goals: Explain the political causes, including the Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh
Describe the socio-religious and economic causes of discontent
Explain the grievances of the sepoys and why the greased cartridges became the immediate cause

slides.heading: The uprising of 1857
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **why** discontent had built up across India by **1857**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: political, socio-religious, economic and military causes, and the spark that set off the uprising
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the summer of eighteen fifty-seven a great uprising shook the rule of the East India Company across northern and central India. It did not come from nowhere. In this part we look at the grievances of rulers, of ordinary people and of the sepoys, and at the rumour that finally set things alight.

slides.heading: Four groups of causes
slides.body_md: Political, socio-religious, economic and military grievances came together.

slides.narration: Historians usually group the causes into four boxes. Rulers and nobles lost power, many people feared for their religion and customs, artisans and peasants grew poorer, and sepoys resented their treatment. When so many groups were unhappy at once, one spark was enough to start a fire.

slides.narration: This schematic timeline shows how the pressure built. Social reforms began in the eighteen twenties, the Doctrine of Lapse was applied from eighteen forty-eight, and Awadh was taken over in eighteen fifty-six. The uprising followed a year later, and in eighteen fifty-eight the Crown took over. The spacing is only a sketch, not an exact scale.

slides.heading: The Doctrine of Lapse
slides.body_md: An **adopted son** was not accepted as heir, so the state **passed to the Company**.

nodes.label: Ruler of a dependent state dies
No natural son; an adopted son is named
Company refuses to accept the adopted heir
The state passes to the Company

visual.alt: Flow of the Doctrine of Lapse: a ruler dies, an adopted son is named because there is no natural son, the Company refuses the adopted heir, and the state passes to the Company
visual.caption: How a state "lapsed".

slides.narration: Indian rulers had long adopted sons when they had none of their own. Under Lord Dalhousie, the Company refused to accept such an adopted son as the next ruler of a dependent state. The state then lapsed, meaning it passed to the Company. Rulers without natural sons began to fear for their thrones.

slides.heading: States taken over
slides.body_md: Lapse and **misgovernment**: two different grounds.

rows: Doctrine of Lapse: adopted heir not recognised
Doctrine of Lapse: adopted heir not recognised
Doctrine of Lapse: adopted heir not recognised

visual.alt: Table of takeovers: Satara in 1848, Jhansi in 1853, Nagpur in 1854 under the Doctrine of Lapse, and Awadh in 1856 on the plea of misgovernment
visual.caption: Two different grounds for takeover.

slides.narration: Satara was the first state taken under the Doctrine, followed by others such as Jhansi and Nagpur. Awadh was different. Its ruler was alive and had been a friend of the Company, but in eighteen fifty-six it was annexed on the plea that it was badly governed. That takeover of a loyal ally caused special bitterness.

slides.heading: Rulers who felt slighted
slides.body_md: Old rulers and their courts saw their **status** swept away.

rows: Nobles and sepoys of Awadh angered
Pension of his adoptive father stopped
Became an opponent of the Company
Successors to lose title and palace

visual.alt: Table of rulers slighted before 1857: the Nawab of Awadh deposed, Nana Saheb denied a pension, the Mughal emperor's successors to lose their title and palace, and rulers without sons unable to pass on their states

slides.narration: Look at how different rulers were treated. The Nawab of Awadh was removed. Nana Saheb, adopted son of the last Peshwa, was refused the pension his father had received. The Mughal emperor was told his successors would lose the imperial title and the palace in Delhi. Each decision created powerful enemies of the Company.

slides.heading: Quick check: Awadh's sepoys
slides.body_md: Did many sepoys of the Bengal Army come from Awadh?
slides.narration: Think about why news from Awadh mattered so much in the army camps.

slides.heading: Fears for religion and custom
slides.body_md: Reforms and missionary work were **seen by some** as interference.

visual.alt: Table of measures seen by some as interference: abolition of sati in 1829, the Religious Disabilities Act of 1850, the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, missionary preaching and schools, and railways and the telegraph
visual.caption: Perceptions of the time, not judgements about the reforms.

slides.narration: Some laws of the period, such as the ban on sati and the law allowing widows to remarry, were welcomed by reformers but disliked by orthodox groups. A law protecting the property of converts, open preaching in bazaars and new schools made many believe that the rulers wanted to change their faith. Even railways, where all castes sat together, worried some people.

slides.heading: Economic distress
slides.body_md: Artisans, peasants and landholders all lost out.

visual.alt: Flow of economic causes: cheap British manufactures undersold Indian handicrafts and left artisans jobless; heavy land revenue pushed peasants into debt and loss of land; wealth flowed to Britain
visual.caption: Economic distress across classes.

slides.narration: Cheap cloth from British mills undersold the work of Indian weavers, who also lost their old patrons when courts were closed. Peasants had to pay high land revenue even in bad years, and many fell into the hands of moneylenders. Wealth flowed out of India to Britain. Economic hardship turned ordinary people against the Company.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting grievances
slides.body_md: Place each imagined person in the right group of causes.
bullets: Step 1: ask what the person **lost**.
Step 2: power or status means **political**; faith or custom means **socio-religious**.
Step 3: livelihood means **economic**; army service means **military**.

rows: A weaver in a market town
Cannot sell cloth against mill-made imports
Fears new laws meddle with marriage and faith
Estate taken over for unpaid revenue
Son told he may be sent overseas
A court official of a lapsed state
Job lost when the state was annexed

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting imagined people by grievance: a weaver (economic), a priest (socio-religious), a taluqdar (economic), a sepoy's family (military) and a court official of a lapsed state (political)
visual.caption: Ask what was lost: power, faith, livelihood or status.

slides.narration: Here are five imagined people. The weaver and the taluqdar lost their livelihood, so theirs are economic grievances. The priest fears for faith and custom, a socio-religious grievance. The sepoy's family worries about service overseas, a military one. The official of an annexed state lost his post through the Company's policy, a political grievance.

slides.heading: Grievances of the sepoys
slides.body_md: Low pay, blocked promotion, **overseas service** and lost allowances.

rows: Lower pay than Europeans; no promotion to high ranks
General Service Enlistment Act (1856) for new recruits
Extra allowance for distant service stopped after annexation
Indian sepoys far outnumbered British soldiers

visual.alt: Table of military grievances: lower pay and no high promotion, compulsory overseas service for new recruits under the 1856 Act, loss of the allowance for distant service, and the large number of Indian sepoys compared with British soldiers

slides.narration: Indian sepoys were the backbone of the Company's army, yet they earned less than European soldiers and could not rise to senior posts. A law of eighteen fifty-six made new recruits promise to serve anywhere, even across the sea, which many feared would cost them their caste. They also lost an extra allowance once distant regions were annexed.

slides.heading: Quick check: the new rifle
slides.body_md: Name the rifle whose cartridges caused the rumour.
slides.narration: A new rifle reached the regiments early in eighteen fifty-seven. What was it called?

slides.heading: The spark: greased cartridges
slides.body_md: A rumour touched **both** Hindu and Muslim sepoys.

nodes.label: Cartridge end had to be bitten
Rumour: greased with cow and pig fat
Hindu and Muslim sepoys refuse the cartridges

visual.alt: Flow of the immediate cause: the Enfield rifle, a cartridge that had to be bitten, the rumour of cow and pig fat, refusal by Hindu and Muslim sepoys, and long-standing anger bursting into revolt
visual.caption: The spark, not the whole fire.

slides.narration: The new Enfield rifle used paper cartridges whose ends had to be bitten off. A rumour spread that they were greased with the fat of cows and pigs, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike. To men already angry, it seemed proof that their religion was under attack. Refusals turned into open revolt in the spring of eighteen fifty-seven.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a ten-mark answer
slides.body_md: Answer in **three parts**: 3 + 3 + 4 marks.

rows: Two causes with a short reason each
Three linked points about one cause
Immediate versus underlying causes; a reasoned view

visual.alt: Worked example table planning a ten-mark answer on the causes: part (i) names two causes in three marks, part (ii) explains one cause in three marks, part (iii) evaluates immediate and underlying causes in four marks

slides.narration: Suppose a question asks about causes in three parts. For three marks, name two causes with a short reason each. For the next three, explain one cause with three linked points. For the last four, compare the spark with the deeper causes and give a reasoned view. One clear point earns one mark.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **Political:** Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh annexed, rulers slighted.
**Socio-religious:** reforms and missionaries seen as interference.
**Economic:** artisans, peasants and landholders ruined.
**Military:** pay, promotion, overseas service, allowances.
**Spark:** greased Enfield cartridges.

nodes.label: Socio-religious: fear of interference and conversion

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: political, socio-religious, economic and military causes, and the greased cartridges as the spark
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Rulers lost their states and status, many feared for their faith, ordinary people grew poorer, and sepoys resented their treatment. The rumour about the greased cartridges was the spark, but the fuel had been gathering for years.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Keep **Awadh** separate from the Doctrine of Lapse: it was annexed for **misgovernment**.
Name the **Enfield rifle** and **both** fats when explaining the cartridges.
Give **examples** with dates: Satara 1848, Jhansi 1853, Awadh 1856.
Distinguish the **immediate cause** from the **underlying causes**.
slides.narration: Some tips. Do not say Awadh lapsed: it was annexed for alleged misgovernment. When you explain the cartridges, name the Enfield rifle and say why both communities were offended. Support causes with examples and dates. And always separate the spark from the deeper causes.

goals: Recall the main centres of the uprising for continuity
Explain how Company rule ended and the new system of administration
State the assurances of Queen Victoria's Proclamation and the changes in policy towards princes and the army

slides.heading: After the storm
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a brief **outline** of the uprising, then its **consequences**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: a brief outline of events for continuity, the end of Company rule, Queen Victoria's Proclamation, the new policy towards princely states and changes in the army
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we first trace, only for continuity, where the uprising spread and who led it. Then we turn to what the examination asks about: how the government of India was reorganised in eighteen fifty-eight, the promises of Queen Victoria's Proclamation, the new policy towards the princes, and the changes in the army.

slides.heading: Outline of events (for continuity only)
slides.body_md: From **Meerut** to Delhi and beyond. *These events are not examined.*

rows: Sepoys rise and march to Delhi

visual.alt: Table of the main centres for continuity only: Meerut where sepoys rose on 10 May 1857, Delhi where Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed, Kanpur with Nana Saheb, Lucknow with Begum Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi with Rani Lakshmibai, and Bihar with Kunwar Singh
visual.caption: For continuity only: events are not examined.

slides.narration: Sepoys at Meerut rose on the tenth of May, eighteen fifty-seven, and marched to Delhi, where the aged Bahadur Shah the Second was proclaimed emperor. Leaders such as Nana Saheb at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Rani Lakshmibai at Jhansi and Kunwar Singh in Bihar joined. The Company regained control by eighteen fifty-eight. This outline is for continuity only.

slides.heading: What should we call it?
columns:
**A revolt of sepoys**

- It **began** in the army.
- It was strongest in **north and central India**.

**A first war of independence**

- **Rulers, peasants and artisans** joined.
- Later nationalists saw it as the **first united struggle**.

rows: Began in the army; strongest in northern and central India
Rulers, peasants and artisans joined against foreign rule

visual.alt: Table of two views about naming the events of 1857: a revolt of sepoys because it began in the army and was strongest in the north and centre, or a first war of independence because rulers, peasants and artisans joined against foreign rule
visual.caption: Historians and nationalists have used both names.

slides.narration: People have named these events differently. Many British writers of the time called it a mutiny, since it started among soldiers and was concentrated in certain regions. Later, Indian nationalist writers called it the first war of independence, because people from many walks of life joined against foreign rule. You should be able to explain both views.

slides.narration: The British Parliament decided that a trading company could no longer govern India. The Government of India Act of eighteen fifty-eight transferred power to the Crown. The Court of Directors and the Board of Control were abolished. A Secretary of State for India, a Cabinet minister, was now in charge in London, advised by the Council of India.

slides.heading: Governor-General and Viceroy
slides.body_md: The head of the government in India now had **two titles**.
bullets: As **Governor-General**, he headed the government of British India.
As **Viceroy**, he represented the **Crown** in dealings with the princes.
He was answerable to the **Secretary of State** in London.
slides.narration: In India the Governor-General continued to head the government, but he now also carried the title of Viceroy, the representative of the Queen. He took his orders from the Secretary of State in London, who in turn answered to Parliament. This chain of control lasted until India became independent.

slides.narration: In November eighteen fifty-eight the Queen's Proclamation was announced in India. In our own words, it promised the princes that their states would not be annexed and their rights would be respected. It promised all Indians freedom of religion and fair entry to government posts on the basis of ability, and it offered pardon to most who had taken part.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: matching promises to groups
slides.body_md: Which group did each assurance reassure most?
bullets: **No annexation** reassured the **princes**.
**Religious freedom** answered the fears behind the **cartridge** rumour and the reforms.
**Equal service** spoke to **educated Indians**.
**Pardon** aimed to calm those who had **taken part**.

slides.narration: Let us connect each promise to the fear it answered. Princes had feared annexation, so they were promised it would stop. Many had feared for their faith, so religious freedom was guaranteed. Educated Indians hoped for government posts, so equal entry was promised. And a pardon was offered to calm those who had fought.

slides.narration: The British noticed that many princes had stayed loyal during the uprising. So the policy changed. Annexation was given up and adopted heirs were accepted. sections.heading: 1. Political causes
sections.body_md:
- **Doctrine of Lapse** (Lord **Dalhousie**, 1848–1856): an **adopted son** was not accepted as heir of a dependent state, so it passed to the Company. Examples: **Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854)**.
- **Awadh** annexed in **1856** on the plea of **misgovernment**; its Nawab, a long-time ally, was deposed.
- **Nana Saheb**, adopted son of the last Peshwa, was refused his father's **pension**.
- The **Mughal emperor's** successors were to lose the **imperial title** and the **Red Fort**.
- Result: rulers and nobles felt **insecure** and **humiliated**.

sections.heading: 2. Socio-religious causes
sections.body_md:
- **Social reforms** such as the abolition of **sati** (1829) and the **Widow Remarriage Act** (1856) were seen by orthodox groups as interference.
- The **Religious Disabilities Act** (1850) let **converts** keep ancestral property; many read it as encouragement to convert.
- **Missionaries** preached and ran schools, and were believed to have official support.
- **Railways** and the **telegraph** were seen by some as breaking **caste** rules.
- These were the **perceptions of the time**; many reforms were also supported by Indian reformers.

sections.heading: 3. Economic causes
sections.body_md:
- **Artisans** ruined by cheap **British manufactures** and the loss of **royal patrons**.
- **Peasants** burdened by **heavy land revenue**, collected strictly; many fell into **debt**.
- **Zamindars and taluqdars** lost estates over unpaid revenue or disputed titles.
- The **drain of wealth**: revenue and profits sent to Britain.

key_terms.definition_md: Transfer of India's wealth to Britain without an equal return.
A landholder who collected revenue from a group of villages.

sections.heading: 4. Military causes and the immediate cause
sections.body_md:
- Sepoys had **lower pay** than European soldiers and could not rise to **high ranks**.
- The **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** required new recruits to **serve anywhere**, including **overseas**.
- The extra **allowance** for service in distant regions stopped when those regions were annexed.
- Indian sepoys **far outnumbered** British troops.
- **Immediate cause:** the cartridges of the new **Enfield rifle**, which had to be bitten, were rumoured to be greased with **cow and pig fat**. Mangal Pandey's attack on officers at **Barrackpore** (March 1857) showed the anger.

sections.heading: 5. Outline of events (for continuity only)
sections.body_md:
- **10 May 1857:** sepoys at **Meerut** rose and marched to **Delhi**; **Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed emperor.
- Other centres: **Kanpur** (Nana Saheb), **Lucknow** (Begum Hazrat Mahal), **Jhansi** (Rani Lakshmibai), **Bihar** (Kunwar Singh).
- The Company regained control by **1858**.
- *Events are studied only for continuity and are not examined.*

sections.heading: 6. Consequences
sections.body_md:
- **Government of India Act, 1858:** Company rule ended; the **Crown** took over. The **Court of Directors** and **Board of Control** were abolished.
- A **Secretary of State for India** (British Cabinet) with a **Council of India**; the **Governor-General** also became the **Viceroy**.
- **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858)**, paraphrased: **no further annexation**; respect for the **rights of princes**; **religious non-interference**; **government posts** open on qualification; **pardon** for most participants.
- **Princes:** annexation given up, **adoption** accepted; princes became **allies** under the Crown's **paramountcy**.
- **Army:** more **European** troops, **artillery** with Europeans, recruitment from groups seen as **loyal**, regiments organised to **divide** communities.

key_terms.definition_md: Representative of the Crown in India.
The supreme authority of the British Crown over the princely states.

questions.stem_md: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, what happened to a dependent Indian state whose ruler died without a natural male heir?

options.text_md: The state passed to the ruler's widow for life
The state passed to the Company, because an adopted son was not accepted as heir
The people of the state elected a new ruler
The state was divided among the neighbouring rulers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The state passed to the Company, because an adopted son was not accepted as heir. The Doctrine refused to recognise an adopted son as successor to the throne, so the state "lapsed" to the Company. The widow, an election or a division among neighbours were not what the policy provided.

questions.stem_md: The Doctrine of Lapse is most closely associated with which Governor-General of the East India Company?

options.text_md: Lord Canning
Lord William Bentinck
Lord Cornwallis
Lord Dalhousie

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lord Dalhousie. Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848–1856) applied the Doctrine to several states. Canning was Governor-General when the uprising began, Bentinck is linked with the abolition of sati, and Cornwallis with an earlier land settlement.

questions.stem_md: Which state was the first to be taken over under the Doctrine of Lapse, in 1848?

options.text_md: Satara
Awadh
Hyderabad
Mysore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Satara. Satara was annexed in 1848. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on a different ground (alleged misgovernment); Hyderabad and Mysore were not taken over in this way.

questions.stem_md: On what ground did the Company annex Awadh in 1856, even though its Nawab had been a long-standing ally?

options.text_md: The Doctrine of Lapse, as the Nawab had no son
Defeat of the Nawab in a war
Alleged misgovernment of the state
A request from the people of Awadh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Alleged misgovernment of the state. Awadh was annexed on the plea that it was badly governed; the Nawab was deposed and sent away. It was not a case of lapse, war or a popular request, which is why the takeover of a loyal ally caused deep resentment.

questions.stem_md: A ruler adopts a son shortly before his death, but the Company refuses to accept the boy and takes over the state. Which state of the 1850s best matches this situation?

options.text_md: Awadh
Punjab
Jhansi
Sindh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Jhansi. Jhansi was taken over in 1853 after the Company refused to recognise the adopted son of the late ruler, a clear use of the Doctrine of Lapse. Awadh was annexed for alleged misgovernment, and Punjab and Sindh were taken after wars.

questions.stem_md: Why did Nana Saheb have a personal grievance against the Company before 1857?

options.text_md: The pension that had been paid to his adoptive father, the last Peshwa, was stopped after the Peshwa's death
His state was annexed for misgovernment
He was dismissed from the Company's army
His lands were confiscated for not paying revenue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The pension that had been paid to his adoptive father, the last Peshwa, was stopped after the Peshwa's death. Nana Saheb was the adopted son of the former Peshwa; the Company refused to continue the Peshwa's pension to him. The other options describe grievances of other groups, not his.

questions.stem_md: How did British policy towards the Mughal emperor in the 1850s add to political discontent?

options.text_md: The emperor was made Governor-General of India
The emperor was given back the provinces of Bengal and Bihar
The emperor was allowed to raise his own large army
It was announced that the emperor's successors would lose the imperial title and the palace in Delhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It was announced that the emperor's successors would lose the imperial title and the palace in Delhi. The Company indicated that after Bahadur Shah II his successors would not keep the imperial title or live in the Red Fort. This hurt those who still saw the Mughal ruler as a symbol of authority. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: An imagined courtier in a small state hears in 1854 that a neighbouring kingdom has lapsed to the Company. What is he most likely to conclude?

options.text_md: That the Company would soon return the kingdom
That no Indian ruler, however loyal, was safe from annexation
That adoption was now encouraged by the Company
That the Company had stopped expanding its territory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That no Indian ruler, however loyal, was safe from annexation. The repeated use of lapse and annexation made rulers feel insecure even if they had been friendly. Nothing suggested the Company would return lands, accept adoption or stop expanding.

questions.stem_md: What was the Doctrine of Lapse? Name two states annexed under it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and two correct states.

answer.model_answer_md: It was the policy, applied vigorously by **Lord Dalhousie**, that a dependent state whose ruler died **without a natural heir** would **pass to the Company**, as an **adopted son** was not accepted. Examples: **Satara** (1848) and **Jhansi** (1853).

questions.stem_md: Why did the annexation of Awadh anger both its people and many sepoys?
questions.solution_md: Injustice to an ally; impact on sepoys.

answer.model_answer_md: Awadh's Nawab had been a **loyal ally**, yet he was **deposed** on a charge of **misgovernment**; nobles and officials **lost their positions**. Many **sepoys came from Awadh**, so the takeover of their **homeland** felt like a **personal injury**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three political causes of the uprising of 1857.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct political causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Doctrine of Lapse:** states such as **Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur** were taken over because **adopted heirs** were not recognised.
2. **Annexation of Awadh (1856)** on a charge of **misgovernment**, though its ruler was an ally.
3. **Treatment of rulers:** **Nana Saheb's pension** was stopped, and the **Mughal emperor's successors** were to lose their title.

questions.stem_md: A law of 1850 allowed a person who changed his religion to keep his share of ancestral property. How did many people of the time see this law?

options.text_md: As a step that would encourage conversion to Christianity
As a reward for loyalty to the Mughal emperor
As a tax on temples
As a measure to help the sepoys

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** As a step that would encourage conversion to Christianity. The Religious Disabilities Act (1850) removed the loss of inheritance on conversion; many feared it was meant to make conversion easier. It had nothing to do with the emperor, temple taxes or the sepoys.

questions.stem_md: Which social reform law passed in 1856 was seen by orthodox sections as interference in their customs?

options.text_md: The Indian Councils Act
The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act
The Vernacular Press Act
The Rowlatt Act

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act. The Widows' Remarriage Act (1856) permitted widows to remarry. The Indian Councils Act, the Vernacular Press Act and the Rowlatt Act came much later.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined town of the 1850s, people notice preachers in the bazaar, new schools teaching Christian scripture and orphans being brought up as Christians. Which cause of the uprising does this illustrate?

options.text_md: The Doctrine of Lapse
The loss of the foreign service allowance
The fear that British rule aimed to convert Indians
The heavy land revenue demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The fear that British rule aimed to convert Indians. Missionary activity, often seen as backed by the rulers, made people fear for their religion. Lapse, the overseas allowance and land revenue are political, military and economic causes.

questions.stem_md: Why did many Indian weavers and other artisans lose their livelihood under Company rule?

options.text_md: The Company paid them very high wages
Indian rulers banned the sale of handmade cloth
The artisans were all recruited into the army
Cheap machine-made British goods flooded Indian markets while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cheap machine-made British goods flooded Indian markets while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain. Machine-made imports undersold handmade goods, and Indian manufactures faced barriers in Britain; the loss of royal courts as patrons made things worse. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: What was the main economic grievance of Indian peasants against the Company before 1857?

options.text_md: Free supply of seeds
Abolition of all taxes on land
Guaranteed prices for their crops
Very high land revenue, collected strictly even in bad years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Very high land revenue, collected strictly even in bad years. Land revenue was fixed high and collected harshly, pushing many into debt or loss of land. Free seeds, abolition of land tax and guaranteed prices did not exist.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the idea of the "drain of wealth" as a cause of discontent?

options.text_md: Indian rulers spent too much on palaces
Rivers were drained to build railways
A large part of India's wealth was sent to Britain as salaries, profits and charges without an equal return
Indian merchants took their money abroad to buy land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A large part of India's wealth was sent to Britain as salaries, profits and charges without an equal return. The drain meant a steady transfer of wealth from India to Britain through the Company's revenue and charges, which impoverished the country. The other options misread the term.

questions.stem_md: In which year was the practice of sati declared illegal in the Bengal Presidency?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1829. Sati was prohibited by a regulation of 1829 under Lord William Bentinck. 1856 is the Widow Remarriage Act and 1858 the end of Company rule.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Some sections of Indian society saw British social reforms as a threat to their religion.

**Reason (R):** They believed that the reforms were part of a plan to change their customs and convert them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true and R explains A: reforms such as permitting widow remarriage were read by orthodox groups as part of a wider design against their faith.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Indian handicraft industries declined in the first half of the nineteenth century.

**Reason (R):** British goods sold in India were taxed far more heavily than Indian goods sold in Britain.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: it was the other way round; British goods entered India on easy terms while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Some people in the 1850s viewed new things such as railways and the telegraph with suspicion, fearing they would break caste rules.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. People of all castes sat together in railway carriages, and such changes were read by some as attacks on social customs.

questions.stem_md: Match each grievance felt before 1857 with the group of causes it belongs to.

options.text_md: A ruler's adopted son is refused the throne
A widow remarriage law upsets orthodox families
A weaver cannot sell cloth against cheap imports
A sepoy is ordered to serve overseas

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Refusal of adoption is political (Doctrine of Lapse); the remarriage law is socio-religious; the weaver's ruin is economic; compulsory overseas service is military.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why many Indians in the 1850s feared for their religion.
questions.solution_md: Any two: missionaries, laws on converts, social reforms seen as interference, new technology seen as breaking caste.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Missionaries** preached openly and ran schools, and many believed the **government supported conversion**.
2. Laws such as the **Religious Disabilities Act (1850)**, protecting the property of **converts**, seemed to **encourage conversion**.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which Company rule hurt the Indian economy before 1857.
questions.solution_md: Any two: artisans, peasants, zamindars losing land, drain of wealth.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Handicrafts** declined as **cheap British manufactures** flooded Indian markets, leaving artisans jobless.
2. **Heavy land revenue**, collected harshly, ruined many **peasants and zamindars**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three socio-religious grievances that prepared the ground for the uprising.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct grievances, each linked to a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Social reforms** such as the abolition of **sati** (1829) and the **Widow Remarriage Act** (1856) were seen by orthodox groups as **interference** in custom.
2. **Missionary activity** and the **Religious Disabilities Act** (1850) created fear of **conversion**.
3. **Western education** and new things like **railways** were believed to **break caste** and undermine traditional ways.

marking_scheme.step: Education or technology seen as threat

questions.stem_md: How did the economic policies of the Company affect artisans, peasants and landholders?
questions.solution_md: One effect for each group.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Artisans:** cheap **British goods** and the loss of **royal patrons** destroyed handicrafts.
2. **Peasants:** **high land revenue**, collected even in bad seasons, drove many into **debt**.
3. **Landholders:** many **zamindars and taluqdars lost their estates** when they could not pay or when titles were questioned.

questions.stem_md: The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 upset many sepoys because it required new recruits to

options.text_md: serve wherever they were sent, including overseas
pay a fee to join the army
give up their pensions
become Christians

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** serve wherever they were sent, including overseas. New recruits had to agree to serve anywhere, including across the sea, which many high-caste sepoys believed would cost them their caste. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes the position of Indian sepoys in the Company's army before 1857?

options.text_md: They were paid more than British officers
They were paid less than British soldiers and could not rise to the highest ranks
They commanded all the artillery units
They could become Commander-in-Chief

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They were paid less than British soldiers and could not rise to the highest ranks. Indian sepoys received lower pay and faced a ceiling on promotion, while senior ranks were kept for Europeans. They did not command the artillery or the army.

questions.stem_md: An imagined sepoy writes home that after a newly annexed region became part of British India, he no longer receives the extra allowance he used to get for serving there. Which grievance is he describing?

options.text_md: The Doctrine of Lapse
The Widow Remarriage Act
The drain of wealth
Loss of the allowance for foreign service (bhatta)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Loss of the allowance for foreign service (bhatta). Sepoys got an extra allowance for service outside British territory; once regions such as Sindh and Punjab were annexed, this allowance stopped. The other options are not military pay grievances.

questions.stem_md: Which new rifle introduced in 1857 is linked with the rumour about greased cartridges?

options.text_md: The Enfield rifle
The Brown Bess musket
The Lee-Metford rifle
The Maxim gun

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Enfield rifle. The Enfield rifle used cartridges whose ends had to be bitten off; the rumour that they were greased with cow and pig fat angered Hindu and Muslim sepoys alike. The other weapons are wrong for this event.

questions.stem_md: Why did the rumour about the new cartridges offend both Hindu and Muslim sepoys?

options.text_md: The cartridges were too expensive to buy
The cartridges were made in Indian factories
The grease was said to contain the fat of cows and pigs, which their religions forbade them to touch with the mouth
The cartridges were too heavy to carry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The grease was said to contain the fat of cows and pigs, which their religions forbade them to touch with the mouth. Cow fat offended Hindus and pig fat offended Muslims, and the cartridge had to be bitten. Cost, place of manufacture and weight were not the issue.

questions.stem_md: At which cantonment did a sepoy of the 34th Native Infantry attack his officers in March 1857, an incident linked to the cartridge issue?

options.text_md: Meerut
Ambala
Barrackpore
Lucknow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Barrackpore. At Barrackpore, near Calcutta, Mangal Pandey attacked officers on 29 March 1857 and was later executed. Meerut was where the large-scale rising began in May 1857.

questions.stem_md: Which fact about the army helps explain why a rising by sepoys could spread so quickly in 1857?

options.text_md: Indian sepoys greatly outnumbered British soldiers, and many British troops were away
Every regiment was commanded by an Indian general
The Company had no soldiers in northern India
All sepoys had been dismissed in 1856

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Indian sepoys greatly outnumbered British soldiers, and many British troops were away. Indian soldiers formed the large majority of the Company's army, and many British units were serving outside India, so sepoys felt strong enough to act. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The issue of the greased cartridges united Hindu and Muslim sepoys.

**Reason (R):** The grease was rumoured to contain fat that was objectionable to both communities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true and R explains A: because the rumour touched both religions, the anger was shared across communities.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 applied only to British soldiers.

**Reason (R):** Many high-caste sepoys believed that crossing the sea would make them lose their caste.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the Act applied to new Indian recruits, who had to agree to serve overseas. R is true, which is why the Act caused alarm.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Before 1857, an Indian sepoy was generally paid less than a British soldier of similar rank.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Pay and allowances favoured European soldiers, and Indians could not rise to the highest ranks.

questions.stem_md: The cartridges of the new ___ rifle were believed to be greased with the fat of cows and pigs.
questions.solution_md: It was the Enfield rifle.

questions.stem_md: State two grievances of Indian sepoys that were not connected with the cartridges.
questions.solution_md: Any two military grievances other than the cartridges.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Low pay and poor promotion**: Indians earned less than Europeans and could not reach high ranks.
2. The **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** forced new recruits to **serve overseas**, which many felt would cost them their caste. (Also: loss of the **foreign service allowance**.)

questions.stem_md: Explain why the greased cartridges became the spark for the uprising.
questions.solution_md: The rumour and why it acted as a trigger.

answer.model_answer_md: Sepoys had to **bite** the cartridge of the new **Enfield rifle**, and it was rumoured to be greased with **cow and pig fat**. This seemed to confirm the fear that the British wanted to **destroy their religion**, so long-standing anger **burst into revolt**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three military causes of the uprising of 1857.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct military causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Discrimination:** Indian sepoys got **lower pay** and could not rise to **senior ranks**.
2. **Overseas service:** the **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** made new recruits liable to serve across the sea.
3. **Loss of allowances:** the **extra allowance** for service in distant regions stopped once those regions were annexed.

questions.stem_md: Which law of 1858 ended the rule of the East India Company in India?

options.text_md: The Regulating Act, 1773
The Charter Act, 1833
The Indian Councils Act, 1861
The Government of India Act, 1858

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Government of India Act, 1858. The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power from the Company to the British Crown. The Regulating Act and Charter Act were earlier, and the 1861 Act dealt with councils.

questions.stem_md: After 1858, which minister in Britain was made responsible for the government of India?

options.text_md: The Chairman of the Court of Directors
The Secretary of State for India
The President of the Board of Control
The Viceroy of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Secretary of State for India. A Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, was created with a Council of India to advise him. The Court of Directors and the Board of Control were abolished; the Viceroy worked in India.

questions.stem_md: What change in the title of the head of the government in India followed the end of Company rule?

options.text_md: The Governor-General was also called the Viceroy, as the representative of the Crown
The Governor-General was replaced by a Prime Minister of India
The office of Governor-General was abolished
The head of government became the Mughal emperor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Governor-General was also called the Viceroy, as the representative of the Crown. The Governor-General now also acted as the Viceroy, the Crown's representative in India. There was no Prime Minister of India, and the office was not abolished.

questions.stem_md: Which assurance in Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 was aimed most directly at the Indian princes?

options.text_md: That they would be given seats in the British Parliament
That there would be no further annexation of their territories and their rights would be respected
That they could keep unlimited armies
That they would choose the Viceroy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That there would be no further annexation of their territories and their rights would be respected. The Proclamation promised to respect the rights and dignity of the princes and to end the policy of annexation. Seats in Parliament, unlimited armies and choosing the Viceroy were never promised.

questions.stem_md: After 1858, an imagined official proposes a rule that would interfere with a religious festival. Which promise of the Queen's Proclamation could people point to against it?

options.text_md: Free education for all children
Abolition of land revenue
Non-interference in the religious beliefs and practices of Indians
Indian control of the army

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Non-interference in the religious beliefs and practices of Indians. The Proclamation promised religious toleration and non-interference. Free education, abolition of land revenue and Indian control of the army were not among its promises.

questions.stem_md: The Proclamation promised that Indians would be admitted to government service. Which condition did it attach?

options.text_md: Admission only for members of princely families
Admission only after converting to Christianity
Admission only for those who had fought in 1857
Admission according to education, ability and integrity, without regard to race or creed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Admission according to education, ability and integrity, without regard to race or creed. The promise was of equal treatment in government service on the basis of qualification, irrespective of race or religion. In practice the high examinations remained difficult for Indians to enter, but the promise itself had no princely, religious or war-service condition.

questions.stem_md: Which change was made in the composition of the army after 1858?

options.text_md: All European soldiers were sent back to Britain
Indian officers were given command of the artillery
The army was disbanded and replaced by the police
The proportion of European soldiers was increased and key branches such as artillery were kept with Europeans

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The proportion of European soldiers was increased and key branches such as artillery were kept with Europeans. The British raised the share of European troops and kept artillery and other key branches in European hands. The other options are the opposite of what happened.

questions.stem_md: After 1858, regiments were organised so that soldiers of different communities and regions were mixed or kept apart in particular ways. What was the main aim?

options.text_md: To give each regiment its own religious leader
To reduce the cost of uniforms
To prevent soldiers from uniting against British rule again
To prepare the army for elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To prevent soldiers from uniting against British rule again. The reorganisation followed a divide-and-rule approach so that soldiers would not combine as in 1857. The other options do not describe the purpose.

questions.stem_md: How did the relationship between the British and the princely states change after 1858?

options.text_md: The princely states became fully independent countries
Annexation stopped and adoption was accepted, but the princes had to accept the Crown as the paramount power
All princely states were annexed within ten years
The princes were given control of British India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Annexation stopped and adoption was accepted, but the princes had to accept the Crown as the paramount power. The British ended annexation and recognised adoption, turning the princes into loyal supporters, but the Crown claimed paramountcy over them. They did not become independent, were not all annexed and did not control British India.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After 1858 the princes generally became supporters of British rule.

**Reason (R):** The Crown gave up the policy of annexation and recognised their right to adopt heirs.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true and R explains A: once their thrones were secure, the princes had a stake in the survival of British rule.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After 1858 the British increased the proportion of European soldiers in India.

**Reason (R):** The Government of India Act, 1858 created the post of Secretary of State for India.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the army change was a security measure after the uprising, while the new post concerned the government in London.

questions.stem_md: True or false? After 1858 the British Crown governed India directly in place of the East India Company.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule and placed India under the Crown.

questions.stem_md: Queen Victoria's Proclamation was announced in India on 1 November ___.
questions.solution_md: It was announced on 1 November 1858.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the chain of authority over India after 1858, from the top in Britain to the head of government in India.

options.text_md: The British Crown and Parliament
The Governor-General and Viceroy in India
The Secretary of State for India, advised by the Council of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (c) → (b). Crown and Parliament at the top; the Secretary of State with the Council of India in London; the Governor-General and Viceroy in India.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two changes in the administration of India made by the Government of India Act, 1858.
questions.solution_md: Any two administrative changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Company rule ended** and India came under the **British Crown**.
2. A **Secretary of State for India**, a British Cabinet minister, was created with a **Council of India**; the **Governor-General** also became the **Viceroy**.

questions.stem_md: Mention two promises made to the Indian people (not the princes) in Queen Victoria's Proclamation.
questions.solution_md: Any two promises to the people.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No interference** in their **religious beliefs** and customs.
2. **Equal opportunity in government service**, on the basis of **qualification**, regardless of race or creed. (Also: a general **pardon** for those not guilty of killing British subjects.)

questions.stem_md: Why did the British change their policy towards the princes after 1858?
questions.solution_md: Reason for the change and what it was.

answer.model_answer_md: Many princes had **stayed loyal** during the uprising, and the British realised they could serve as **dependable allies** against future revolts. So annexation was **given up** and **adoption accepted**, binding the princes to the Crown.

questions.stem_md: State two changes made in the army after the uprising.
questions.solution_md: Any two changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **proportion of European soldiers** was increased.
2. **Artillery** and other key branches were kept with **Europeans**; recruitment shifted to groups seen as **loyal**, and regiments were organised to **divide** communities.

questions.stem_md: The events of 1857 have been called a "mutiny" by some writers and the "First War of Independence" by others. Give one reason for each view.
questions.solution_md: One reason for each view, stated neutrally.

answer.model_answer_md: **Mutiny:** it **began among sepoys** in the Company's army and was strongest in **northern and central India**. **War of Independence:** it drew in **rulers, peasants and artisans** with a shared aim of **ending foreign rule**, and later nationalists saw it as the **first united struggle**.

marking_scheme.step: Reason for the "war of independence" view

questions.stem_md: Explain three main assurances given in Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858.
questions.solution_md: Three assurances, paraphrased.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No more annexation**; the **rights and dignity of the princes** and existing **treaties** would be respected.
2. **Religious toleration**: no interference in the **beliefs and customs** of Indians.
3. **Equal opportunity** in **government service** on merit, and a **pardon** for most of those who had taken part, except those who had killed British subjects.

questions.stem_md: Describe three changes in the organisation of the army after 1857 and the purpose behind them.
questions.solution_md: Three changes with their purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **share of European troops** was raised, so that Indian soldiers could not again **outnumber** them heavily.
2. **Artillery** and important **arsenals** were kept under **Europeans**, denying Indians the most powerful weapons.
3. Recruitment favoured groups considered **loyal**, and regiments were organised on **community and caste lines** to **divide and rule**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the political background of 1857.

(i) What was the Doctrine of Lapse? Name the Governor-General associated with it and two states annexed under it. **[3]**
(ii) Explain why the annexation of Awadh caused anger. **[3]**
(iii) How did the treatment of Nana Saheb and of the Mughal emperor add to political discontent? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Doctrine of Lapse; Awadh; Nana Saheb and the Mughal emperor.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was the policy that a dependent state whose ruler died **without a natural male heir** would **lapse to the Company**, since an **adopted son** was not recognised. It is linked with **Lord Dalhousie**; examples are **Satara** and **Jhansi** (also Nagpur).

(ii) Awadh was annexed in **1856** on the plea of **misgovernment**, although its Nawab had been a **loyal ally**. Nobles and officials lost their positions, and the many **sepoys from Awadh** felt their homeland had been seized.

(iii) **Nana Saheb**, adopted son of the last **Peshwa**, was refused the **pension** paid to his father, so he became an opponent of the Company. The Company announced that the **successors of the Mughal emperor** would lose the **imperial title** and the **Red Fort**, which offended those who still respected the emperor as a **symbol of authority**. Both showed that the Company **ignored old rulers**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the social and economic background of 1857.

(i) Explain three social reforms or laws that some Indians saw as interference in their religion. **[3]**
(ii) Why did missionary activity cause fear among Indians? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how British economic policies affected artisans and peasants. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Reforms; missionaries; artisans and peasants.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **abolition of sati** (1829), the **Widow Remarriage Act** (1856) and the **Religious Disabilities Act** (1850), which let **converts** keep ancestral property, were read by orthodox groups as attacks on **custom and faith**.

(ii) Missionaries **preached openly**, ran **schools** that taught Christian scripture and brought up **orphans as Christians**; since many believed the **government supported** them, people feared a plan of **mass conversion**.

(iii) **Artisans** lost their market to cheap **machine-made British goods** and lost the patronage of **royal courts**; **peasants** faced **heavy land revenue**, collected strictly even in bad years, and many fell into **debt** or lost their land to **moneylenders**. This **economic distress** made both groups ready to join the revolt.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the sepoys and 1857.

(i) State three grievances of Indian sepoys in the Company's army. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 affected the sepoys. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why the greased cartridges became the immediate cause of the uprising. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Grievances; the 1856 Act; the cartridges as trigger.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Lower pay** than British soldiers; **no promotion** beyond a low rank; **loss of the allowance** for service in distant regions once they were annexed.

(ii) The Act required **new recruits** to agree to **serve anywhere**, including **overseas**. Many high-caste sepoys believed **crossing the sea** would make them **lose caste**, so they felt their **religion** was under threat and feared for future recruitment of their sons.

(iii) The new **Enfield rifle** used cartridges whose ends had to be **bitten**; it was rumoured they were greased with **cow and pig fat**, offending **both Hindus and Muslims**. Coming after many other grievances, the rumour seemed to **prove** that the British meant to **destroy their faith**, and sepoys refused the cartridges, which turned **anger into open revolt**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the changes in administration after 1857.

(i) Which law ended the rule of the East India Company, and when? **[3]**
(ii) Explain the new arrangement for governing India from Britain. **[3]**
(iii) State four assurances given in Queen Victoria's Proclamation. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: The 1858 Act; Secretary of State and Viceroy; four assurances.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred the government of India from the **East India Company** to the **British Crown**; the **Court of Directors** and the **Board of Control** were abolished.

(ii) A **Secretary of State for India**, a member of the **British Cabinet** answerable to **Parliament**, took charge, advised by a **Council of India**. In India the **Governor-General** governed as the **Viceroy**, the representative of the Crown.

(iii) **No further annexation**; respect for the **rights and dignity of the princes** and their **treaties**; **no interference in religion**; **equal opportunity in government service** on merit regardless of race or creed; a **pardon** for most participants except those who had killed British subjects.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Act and transfer to the Crown

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about British policy after 1857.

(i) How did the British change their policy towards the princely states? **[3]**
(ii) Why did they make this change? **[3]**
(iii) Explain four changes made in the army and how each was meant to prevent another revolt. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Policy change; reasons; four army changes with purposes.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The policy of **annexation**, including the **Doctrine of Lapse**, was **given up**; the princes' **right to adopt** heirs was accepted, but they had to recognise the **Crown as the paramount power**.

(ii) Many princes had **stayed loyal** or neutral in 1857, and the British saw them as **useful allies** who would help keep the people under control; securing their thrones gave them a **stake in British rule**.

(iii) The **proportion of European troops** was raised so Indians could not outnumber them heavily; **artillery** was kept with **Europeans** so rebels would lack heavy guns; recruitment favoured groups seen as **loyal**; and regiments were organised on **community and caste lines** to **divide** soldiers and stop them uniting.

marking_scheme.step: (i) End of annexation and acceptance of adoption

questions.stem_md:
A student says the uprising of 1857 happened only because of the greased cartridges.

(i) Give one political and one economic cause that show discontent existed before 1857. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how socio-religious fears made the cartridge rumour so powerful. **[3]**
(iii) Do you agree with the student? Give reasons for your answer. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Earlier causes; link of fears to the rumour; reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Political:** the **Doctrine of Lapse** and the **annexation of Awadh** made rulers and nobles hostile. **Economic:** **artisans** were ruined by British imports and **peasants** burdened by **heavy land revenue**.

(ii) Reforms on **sati** and **widow remarriage**, the law protecting **converts**, and open **missionary activity** had already convinced many that the British wanted to **change their religion**; so when told the cartridges were greased with **cow and pig fat**, sepoys believed it at once.

(iii) **Disagree** (a reasoned view): the cartridges were the **immediate cause**, the **spark**, but the revolt spread to **rulers, peasants and artisans** because of **long-standing political, economic, social and military grievances**. Without these, the cartridge issue alone might have stayed a **local protest** by sepoys.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Link between fears and the rumour

Answer the following about the results of 1857.

(i) Explain the end of Company rule and the new title of the Governor-General. **[3]**
(ii) Explain any three promises of Queen Victoria's Proclamation. **[3]**
(iii) Describe how the uprising changed British policy towards the princely states and the army. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: End of Company rule; three promises; princes and army.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Under the **Government of India Act, 1858**, the **Company's rule ended** and the **Crown** took direct charge; the **Governor-General** was now also the **Viceroy**, ruling in the name of the Crown.

(ii) **No further annexation** and respect for the **rights of the princes**; **no interference in religion**; **equal opportunity in government service** on the basis of qualification.

(iii) **Princes:** annexation was given up and **adoption** accepted, making the princes **loyal allies** under the Crown's **paramountcy**. **Army:** more **European soldiers**, **artillery** kept with Europeans, recruitment from groups seen as **loyal**, and regiments organised to **divide** communities.
